author: Randi Beers
title: Blubber for bibles
content:
Greenlanders were the first Inuit to have the Christian Bible translated into their language.




Between 1750 and 1850, Danish and Norwegian ministers of the Lutheran Church and German Moravians worked to translate the scriptures into Kalaallisut. They were aided by the Danish Bible Society and the London-based British and Foreign Bible Society.




By 1850, there were at least 20 versions of the Bible in existence. Some were more accurate than others. As missionaries’ knowledge of the language progressed, the translations became better.




The writing systems used also posed a problem. The Greenlandic orthography had not yet been standardized. It would remain for Samuel Kleinschmidt, son of a Moravian missionary, to undertake that task in the 1850s.




The Qallunaat ministers could not, of course, have taken on the monumental task of translating into a language new to them without the assistance of Inuit converts to Christianity who were willing, and usually eager, to help them.




Before 1800, the New Testament and some psalms had been translated by Paul Egede, son of Hans Egede, who had established the first mission in Greenland in 1721. Paul Egede had the advantage of having grown up in Greenland and therefore spoke Greenlandic much better than his father did.




Paul Egede did not mention the names of his Greenlandic assistants when his first translations were published in 1744. We only learn their names through his journal, published more than four decades later, in 1788.
















His main assistants were a woman, Arnarsak, baptized in 1737, and a man, Pungiok, who took the Christian name of Hans.




The two made an unusual request of Egede. They did not want the translations, for which they were in part responsible, to be shared widely among the Kalaallit.




Egede explained their reasoning: “It would not be useful for their unbelieving compatriots to be made aware, for example, that Cain, one of God’s first rational creations, was so wicked, or of Jacob’s deception of his father and brother, [or] the polygamy of the patriarchs.”




The two Greenlanders suggested that, instead, only certain selections from the translations should be distributed and that the more lurid parts be omitted. Nonetheless, the translations were published in their entirety.




The Moravians in Greenland were off to a slower start with biblical translations. In the late 1700s, they expended their mission efforts to Labrador where they built on the strengths of missionaries to that coast who brought with them the knowledge they had acquired in Greenland.




In 1804, the British and Foreign Bible Society was formed, with a daunting mandate to translate the Bible into all the languages of the world. Within a century, their publications were available in over 1,000 languages.
















In Labrador, the Inuit Moravian converts eagerly accepted the British and Foreign Bible Society’s publications of the Gospel, as translated by their missionaries, who usually worked by revising Greenlandic publications into their understanding of the local dialect.




Grateful Inuit wrote letters of thanks to the society. Brother Benjamin Kohlmeister sent some of these letters from Nain to Rev. C. J. Latrobe, who provided them to the society.




The Labrador Inuit, unprompted, decided to make a collection of seal blubber to send to the society to help in the costs of its work. They knew that blubber was a valuable trade commodity at the Moravian stores — the Moravians supported the costs of their missions through trade with the Inuit.




Kohlmeister wrote: “Some brought whole seals, others half a seal or pieces, as they could spare it. Some brought pieces of blubber in the name of their children, requesting that their poor gifts might be accepted.”




The Inuit had learned that the society’s work was supported through donations from pious people, who were often poor.
















They explained, through Kohlmeister: “We have indeed spoken together, and observed, that these many books, given to us without pay, must be very dear somewhere, but we never have known before now, that even poor people bring their money, out of pure love, that we may get these comfortable words of God. We are indeed poor, but we might bring now and then some blubber as a contribution.”




The blubber yielded 30 gallons of oil. Kohlmeister went on: “They now begged me to send this collection of blubber to those generous friends who printed the Bibles for them, that more heathen might be presented with that book.”




A careful reading makes it clear what the Inuit intended. They were not offering the blubber to pay for the books they had received “without pay.”




Rather, they were offering to support the society in its translations of the Bible into other languages far removed from the Moravian missions to the Inuit.




The Inuit in Labrador saw themselves as part of a worldwide community of Christians.




[Note: I owe the title to a scholarly paper by Hilary Mary Carey of the University of Bristol. It was too good a title to pass up.]




Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

title: Pirutsiagutiit ends Inuit Child First Initiative uncertainty
content:
It’s welcome news the federal government has finally ended the uncertainty around its Inuit Child First Initiative that has existed for two years. But there’s still a lot of work to be done to see how its $115-million-a-year replacement will work as Ottawa transfers responsibility to four Inuit treaty organizations.

Pirutsiagutiit

The government created it to provide health, social and education products, services and supports to address what Obed called the “profound inequities” Inuit children face. It has been nearly a year since Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty pledged to

title: Lack of security guard rules could expose GN, professor says
content:
The Government of Nunavut could be sued if unregulated private security guards in the territory break the law, says a criminologist, who studies surveillance and security regulation.




That’s because Nunavut has no legislation that governs the training and certification of security guards.




“What are they waiting for? I don’t understand the rationale for not pursuing it and passing it into law,” University of Windsor professor Randy Lippert said in a phone interview.




The government does not appear to share that sense of urgency.




It has received calls to enact regulation during sessions of the legislative assembly in 2018, 2023 and 2025.




The latest call for regulation came from current Justice Minister George Hickes during the winter 2025 sitting of the legislative assembly, about 10 months before he joined cabinet.




He also highlighted the need for Nunavummiut to be hired in security roles.

ᐅᓇ $500 ᒥᓕᐊᓐᑐᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᓄᒃᑭᒃᓴᐅᑎᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ, ᒫᓐᓇᓕ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᖓᓂᐊᕐᓂᖓ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓪᓗᓂ, ᑐᒃᓯᕋᐅᓯᐅᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᓄᒃᑭᒃᓴᐅᑏᑦ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂ, ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᕿᑭᖅᑖᓗᒃ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᓐᓄ, ᑖᒃᑯᐊᓗ ᕿᑭᖅᑕᓂ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᓄᑦ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓕᕆᓪᓗᓂᔾᔪᒃ.




ᐊᖏᖅᑕᐅᒍᓂ ᓴᓇᓯᒋᐊᕐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᓄᒃᑭᒃᓴᐅᑎᖃᖅᕕᒃᓴᒥ ᑰᖕᒥᙶᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᒪᕐᒧᑦ ᓴᖏᓂᖃᓕᕈᓐᓇᕐᓗᓂ 30 ᒥᒐᕗᐊᑦᔅ ᐅᕙᓂ ᑰᒑᓗᒃ ᑰᖕᒥᑦ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ 60 ᑭᓛᒥᐊᓂ ᐅᖓᓯᖕᓂᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐅᐊᖕᓇᖓᑕ ᑲᓇᖕᓇᖅᐸᓯᐊᓂ ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ. ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᖅ 7,136 ᕼᐊᒃᑎᐊ ᐃᒪᖃᖅᕕᒃᒥ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ 66 ᑭᓛᒥᑕ ᐊᖅᑯᑎᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᒥᑦ.




ᑖᓐᓇ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᓄᒃᑭᒃᓴᐅᑎᖃᕐᕕᒃᓴᖅ ᐃᓇᖏᕐᓯᓇᔭᕐᓂᖓᓂ 15 ᒥᓕᐊᓐ ᓖᑕᓂ ᐅᕐᓱᐊᓗᒃ ᑏᓱᒥ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑕᒫᓐ ᐆᒻᒪᖅᑯᑎᖃᕐᕕᒃᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᒃᑐᒥ.

title: Bill C-10 becomes law, creates modern treaty watchdog
content:
A federal bill to create an independent watchdog to monitor Canada’s implementation of modern treaties was passed into law Thursday.




The Land Claims Agreements Coalition welcomed the news, calling it “an important step” toward independent oversight of modern treaties, which are agreements between Indigneous Peoples and the government since 1975.




“For more than 20 years, Inuit and other Modern Treaty partners have called for independent oversight of our agreements. Today, we have taken an important step toward making that a reality,” Gloria Uluqsi, the organization’s co-chair, said in a news release. She is also president of Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. 




The Land Claims Agreement Coalition represents 23 Inuit and First Nations modern treaty holders, including NTI and Makivvik.




Modern treaties, also known as comprehensive land claims agreements signed after 1975, define land and resource rights between Indigenous signatories and the Crown.




The Commissioner for Modern Treaty Implementation Act establishes an independent commissioner who will review federal government activities related to treaty implementation, conduct performance audits and report his or her findings to Parliament.




Federal departments and the auditor general will, however, remain responsible for meeting Canada’s treaty obligations, the news release said.

title: Nunavik communities elect new school board commissioners
content:

The election results were announced Wednesday. Representatives were elected in 13 of the region’s 14 communities, a press release issued Wednesday by Nunavik’s school board said.




The election in Kangiqsujuaq was postponed to Thursday for logistical reasons, communications director Jade Duchesneau-Bernier said in an email.




Several candidates were elected by acclamation, including Adamie Alayco in Akulivik, Nancy Palliser in Inukjuak and Sarah Aloupa in Quaqtaq.




Ten commissioners were elected in contested races, including Charlie Akpahatak (Aupaluk), Evie Mark Kalingo (Ivujivik), McCombie Annanack (Kangiqsualujjuaq), Peter Annahatak Timmons (Kangirsuk), Eva Kauki (Kuujjuaq), Jeannie Aragutak (Kuujjuaraapik), Jacqueline Amamatuak (Puvirnituq), Patsy Cameron (Salluit), Mary Berthe (Tasiujaq) and Noah Inukpuk (Umiujaq).

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Garbage truck fire caused by ‘suspected’ lithium-ion battery
content:
A garbage truck fire believed to have been caused by a lithium-ion battery prompted the City of Iqaluit to remind residents to take care when sorting their garbage.




The truck was on its regular route Wednesday when it caught fire while collecting waste on Joamie Court near Tundra Buddies Daycare,  a public service announcement issued later that day said.




“Crews responded quickly by unloading the waste onto the roadway to prevent the situation from escalating,” the announcement said.




While the fire’s cause has not been confirmed, officials suspect it was related to the improper disposal of lithium-ion, or rechargeable, batteries.




Lithium-ion batteries can spark fires when crushed, punctured or overheated, sometimes leading to explosions that can ignite nearby paper, cardboard and or debris, the announcement said.




The city issued a 

similar reminder

 in July after a fire at the city’s landfill. As well, in August 2024, a fire 

caused

 by a laptop left overheating on a bed caused damage to a Rankin Inlet home.




Iqaluit residents are advised to discard lithium-ion batteries at the safe disposal site at the city’s landfill.
















The city is also creating plans for additional drop-off locations for hazardous waste, Coun. Kyle Sheppard said Wednesday in a Facebook post.

title: Nunavut Arctic College to offer its own teaching degree
content:
Nunavut Arctic College is expected to offer its own credited bachelor of education program next fall.




“We have the skills, we have the knowledge, we have the administrative mechanisms to support the program,” said president Jackie Price in an interview. “So it’s time.”




The college’s current equivalent is offered in partnership with Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, through a program that allows students to complete their studies remotely from Nunavut. Prior versions of the program included the University of Regina and McGill University in Montreal.




Due to funding restraints, the college will offer the new program in Iqaluit and up to four other communities to start, though its administration is still assessing which ones, Price said.




In 2021, the college received more than $34 million for its education program, through a five-year agreement between Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. and the territorial and federal governments.




That money allowed the program to expand to 21 communities through remote learning, Price said. But the funding has run out.

title: Woman found dead in cabin fire nearRankin Inlet
content:
Rankin Inlet RCMP and the Nunavut fire marshal’s office are investigating after a woman was found dead in a cabin fire outside the community early Sunday morning.




Police were called to an area outside the community called Johnson’s Cove at around 2:15 a.m. Sunday, RCMP said Tuesday in a news release.




Rankin Inlet fire fighters extinguished the fire and found a woman inside the cabin.

The Nunavut coroner’s office is also assisting in the investigation.

author: David Venn
title: RCMP conducts ‘largest drug seizure destined for Nunavut’
content:
In what the RCMP calls “the largest drug seizure destined for Nunavut,” police seized five kilograms of cocaine in southern Canada in August, a news release issued Tuesday says.




As a result, an estimated 50,000 doses (measuring one-tenth of a gram) were prevented from entering the territory, the release said.




“This seizure represents far more than the removal of drugs from the supply chain,” Chief Supt. Kent Pike said in the release. “It represents lives protected, families spared from harm and fewer opportunities for organized crime to profit at the expense of Nunavummiut.”




In February 2026, the police force began investigating an alleged money-laundering and drug-trafficking operation.




In August, officers from Nunavut and the federal Arctic unit executed a search warrant in Ottawa, where they seized the drugs.




The federal Arctic unit works under the Federal Policing Northwest Region, which co-ordinates resources to investigate organized crime in Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, Saskatchewan and Nunavut.




The release did not say if any charges have been laid. It said the investigation is ongoing and that the RCMP will not provide further comment.

The girls’ grandparents are planning to head to Kimmirut Friday from Kinngait to support the parents, Elisapie Pootoogook said.




Kimmirut has a population of approximately 400 people.




The community’s school and daycare were closed Monday out of respect for those affected by the girls’ deaths.
















South Baffin MLA David Joanasie, whose riding includes Kimmirut and Kinngait, shared his support for the family Monday in a Facebook post.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: GN, University of Ottawa partner to train doctors in Iqaluit
content:
The Government of Nunavut is partnering with the University of Ottawa to train family medicine residents in Iqaluit, in an effort to improve access to primary care and encourage more doctors to practise in the territory.




Health Minister Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster announced the five-year agreement Monday at the university’s Faculty of Medicine.




The new Nunavut-uOttawa Family Medicine Residency Stream will bring four medical residents to Iqaluit in 2027, with another four expected to join in 2028, said a University of Ottawa news release.




The program will reach a capacity of eight residents in its second year, the release said.




Residents complete two months of clinical rotations in Iqaluit during their first year of residency and five months during their second year. 

The GN will fund the residency positions.




“The valued knowledge, expertise, and collaborations that medical residents will experience in Iqaluit will be shared within our community of learners to open broader perspectives on training, care, and research,” University of Ottawa president and vice-chancellor Marie-Eve Sylvestre said in the news release.

author: David Venn
title: Nunavut coroner schedules inquest into Rankin Inlet man’s death
content:
Nunavut’s chief coroner has scheduled an inquest into the death of a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man who was shot and killed by police five years ago.




The inquest is set for Nov. 23 to 27 at Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet, the Office of the Chief Coroner announced in a public service announcement Monday.




“The purpose of this inquest is to explore the circumstances surrounding the death of Mr. Trey Angootealuk,” the announcement states, “and to consider recommendations to prevent death in similar circumstances.”




On the afternoon

 of Nov. 6, 2021, RCMP officers responded to a call for a disturbance that involved “intoxicated males,” according to a police report at the time.




Angootealuk walked around town with a rifle, shot toward police officers, hijacked a truck at gunpoint and drove to the outskirts of town, where police contained him for several hours before shooting him.




In May 2022, the Ottawa Police Service, which investigates major incidents that involve Nunavut RCMP, found that there were 

no grounds

 to believe any officer committed a crime.




Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved in the incident.
















Anyone who would like to participate in the inquest can contact the territory’s coroner’s office at 867-975-6562

title: Various Molson, Coors beer brands under nationwide recall
content:
A national food recall for several brands of beer due to “metal contamination” does not affect products on Nunavut’s beer and wine store shelves, the Finance Department announced Friday.




The recall was first announced Nov. 9 due to the possible presence of small pieces of metal inside the affected products.




Various beers produced by Molson Coors Beverage Co. are affected, including Coors Light, Molson Canadian and Blue Moon Belgian-Style Wheat Ale.




The only non-alcoholic beverages on the list are six- and 24-packs of Non-Alcoholic Blue Moon Belgian-Style Wheat Ale.




The exact items, including packaging and UPC codes, 

can be found

 on the Canadian Health Inspection Agency website.




None of the alcoholic beverages listed are in the Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission’s current inventory, according to the announcement from the Finance Department.




Non-alcoholic beers are available in grocery stores. Consumers are urged not to sell, distribute or drink products included on the list.

content:

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Senate bill would let police intercept drugs sent by mail
content:
A bill recently introduced in the Senate would give police, including Nunavut’s RCMP, new powers to intercept suspected drug shipments moving through the postal system before they reach their destinations, says the territory’s RCMP commander.




“Bill S-8 doesn’t create unrestricted access to the mail, and it does not allow postal inspectors to open things. Existing safeguards remain in place,” Chief Supt. Kent Pike said Friday in an interview.




“The difference now, if this bill is approved, is that I will still have a warrant, but I will be allowed to stop the package before it gets to its destination.”




The proposed changes are part of Bill S-8, the Combatting Financial Crimes and Drug Trafficking Act, introduced in the Senate Nov. 3 by Sen. Pierre Moreau.




The bill would amend the Canada Post Corporation Act to allow law enforcement agencies to search and seize mail when authorized under the Criminal Code, the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act or the Cannabis Act.




Pike said the postal system has become an attractive option for drug trafficking because packages can be difficult to trace.




“It’s evident right now, based on the fact that we can’t even touch the mail system, that for people who ship illegal substances, this is the least risky way for them to be caught as opposed to bringing it in on your person or sending it by cargo,” Pike said.

author: Randi Beers
title: Nunavut Housing Corp. distances itself from NCCD partnership
content:
Once billed as the “biggest business development opportunity” in NCC Development Ltd.’s history, a 10-year agreement for the company to build up to 2,000 housing units in Nunavut by 2030 is stalled.




Instead, Nunavut Housing Corp. is working with construction company NCCD to make sure the initial 316 units NCCD signed on to deliver as part of its first two contracts with the housing corporation are built.




“As a result of the significant delays and logistical issues that have been encountered as part of our agreement with NCCD, no new contracts are being awarded to [the company] for the 2026-27 fiscal year,” said Nathan Carter, spokesperson for Nunavut Housing Corp., Nov. 6 in an email.




NCCD was awarded one contract in 2025 to build two houses in Apex as part of a separate pilot project, Carter said.

initiative

author: Corey Larocque
title: Let’s hope ‘build, baby, build’ doesn’t overshadow environmental protection
content:
We’re starting to see what it means to be “masters of our destiny,” to “build Canada strong” and to “build, baby, build.”




Those are expressions associated with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s bullish approach to strengthening Canada’s economy in the face of uncertainty by building big infrastructure projects — and building them fast.




Two recent Nunavut-related steps signal a willingness to ease off conventional safeguards in the interest of stimulating the economy. Carney’s Liberal government is considering 

lifting the moratorium

 on oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. And its adviser on the impact of proposed developments in Nunavut says the proposed Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project does not require a 

public review

.




In 2016, a Liberal government under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau imposed a ban on offshore oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. The risk of spillage could be disastrous to a delicate ecosystem and pristine wilderness.




But when Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne unveiled the 2026-27 budget on Nov. 5, it included funding that will be used to consider lifting that ban. Since taking over as prime minister in 2025, Carney has relaxed his party’s environmental protection standards in favour of strengthening the economy by building so-called “nation-building” infrastructure projects.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqlauit gets sneak peek at Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre
content:
Nunavut’s $83.7-million Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre gave the public its first look inside Friday, approximately seven months before staff will welcome the first 24 full-time residents inside.




Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. President Gloria Uluqsi, left, says she looks forward to the leadership provided by Annie Aningmiuq, executive director of Aqqusariaq Corp., the arms-length nonprofit organization established to run the centre. (Photo by Daron Letts)




Hiring, trauma-informed care training for new staff, programming decisions, and operational preparations continue before services can be delivered, said Annie Aningmiuq, executive director of 

Aqqusariaq Corp., the arms-length nonprofit organization established by Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. to run the centre.




However, outpatient care will begin early in the new year, she added, during an interview.




“

We have a gorgeous sewing room – we can have cultural programming here before we have people living upstairs to do their their treatments

,” she said. “We can also connect other services that are available.”




The facility also features a classroom, withdrawal recovery rooms, a nursing station and exam room, a cultural food processing area, a daycare, and a group therapy room. Inuit art is displayed throughout the building.




So far, two other employees have been hired, with three more core positions to be filled in coming

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Narwhal, seals and more adorn University of Ottawa wall
content:
Aija Komangapik painted a grey seal as part of a mural project at the University of Ottawa because it is an animal she knows well.




Cyclists ride past as Inuk artist Aija Komangapik looks at a new collaborative mural along a bike pathway at the University of Ottawa in Ottawa on Nov. 5. Komangapik was one of five Indigenous artists from across Canada who painted sections of the campus project. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




“The grey seal is the one I catch, the one I use to prepare sealskins. It’s the one I hunt to provide people with meat,” said the 28-year-old artist and hunter.




She included the animal in her section of a new mural on the wall beside the university’s train station entrance, which also serves as a bike pathway.




Her section begins with a painting of the sea goddess Sedna’s severed fingers, which then leads to illustrations of a blue whale, a two-tusk narwhal, a beluga whale, a walrus and seals.




“The creation for all the animals starts in the ocean, and for Inuit, it starts with Sedna,” she said on Nov. 5, while standing in front of the mural as cyclists sped past.







Komangapik, who was born in Iqaluit but now lives in Ottawa, began hunting on the water in her 20s, after she moved down south when she was 12.
















“I’ve been feeling very close to my culture again and hunting has really helping me get back in touch with myself,” she said

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: John Amagoalik squares off with GN in court over home-care funding
content:
Nunavut Chief Justice Susan Cooper reserved her decision after hearing lawyers for John Amagoalik argue the territorial government should pay for his private medical care in Iqaluit while government lawyers argued it shouldn’t.




Lawyers for the man many consider the “Father of Nunavut” were in civil court Friday, trying to secure emergency funding to allow him to receive medical care in Iqaluit while 

a lawsuit

 he brought against the Nunavut government proceeds.




At issue is the retired politician’s request for approximately $16,000 a month to pay for private support care workers and housing.




Amagoalik says he needs that money so he can live with his wife and family in Iqaluit instead of at a long-term care facility in Ottawa, where he had been living for a year and a half until he returned North in August.




Nunavut’s Health Department has declined the request, saying it’s outside the government’s 

legislative authority

 to provide the amount of in-home care Amagoalik needs to stay in Nunavut.




Last month, Amagoalik, 79, 

filed an application

 for a judicial review of the Health Department’s decision, which the court will consider at a later date.




The department has so far offered to cover two hours a week of private support care for Amagoalik, which his lawyer Dougald E. Brown said is unacceptable. He currently receives up to 10 hours of care a day.

.







ᓱᕋᒃᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᕕᖃᕐᒪᓐ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᙳᖅᑎᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᒪᓕᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᖃᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ, ᐃᓚᖏᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒐᓴᖕᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᑐᕐᓯᒪᓂᑰᔪᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᑦ.




“ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᖏᑦ ᐱᔭᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᖏᑦ ᓄᖅᑲᖅᓯᒪᙱᒻᒪᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕆᐊᕐᕕᐅᕙᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᔨᐅᕆᒥ ᔭᖕ, ᐊᓈᓇᖓᓂ ᐱᔭᐅᓂᑯ ᓱᕈᓯᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ. “ᑲᔪᓰᓐᓇᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᐅᓕᕌᖓᑕ.”




ᔭᖕ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᕐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓄᑦ ᐊᑐᖃᑦᑕᖅᓯᒪᔭᕕᓂᕐᒥᓂᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥᑦ ᓄᕕᐱᕆ 5-ᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᑭᖑᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓂᒃ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᑉ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕈᓯᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ.




ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᓚᕐᑐᒥ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ, ᑕᓪᓕᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑦ 15 ᐃᓗᐊᓂ, ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᖅᓯᒪᓗᐊᒋᓐᓂᖓᓂ. ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᓗᐊᙱᒻᒪᑕ ᖃᔅᓯᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂ, ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖃᑦᑕᙱᓗᐊᖅᖢᑎᒡᓗ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᕆᒐᓗᐊᖅᖢᒍ ᑕᒪᒃᑯᐊ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᒃᑐᒥᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᐊᕋᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑕ.




ᔭᖕ, ᒫᓐᓇ 26-ᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᖃᓕᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᓈᓇᖓᓂ ᐱᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐸᓐᓂᕐᑑᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᑦᑎᐊᕋᓱᒃᑲᓗᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᔭᖕ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᓗᐊᕋᓱᒋᓚᐅᕐᑕᖓ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓗᐊᖅᑐᒦᓐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓂᕿᖃᕈᓐᓇᑦᑎᐊᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᓚᒌᑦ, ᐅᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐊᓈᓇᖓ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓂ 12-ᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᑖᕋᓱᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᓂᖓᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐊᔪᖅᑎᑕᐅᖏᓐᓇᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ.
















“ᓄᓇᖃᑎᒌᓕᕆᔩᑦ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᙱᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᔪᕐᓴᑲᑕᓗᐊᖅᐳᒍᑦ. ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᒃᓱᕈᕐᓇᖅᑐᒃᑰᑲᑕᓚᐅᖅᑐᒍᑦ.”




ᔭᖕ ᐃᓱᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖅ ᒐᕙᒪᖃᕐᓂᖓ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ. ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᑐᓕᕆᔨ ᐲᑕ ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᓖᓐ ᕼᐊᓯ, ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒐᓴᖕᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᔪᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᖅᐸᒃᖢᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᕐᓇᖏᓐᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ.




ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅ

author: Randi Beers
title: Fresh face in cabinet expected to receive portfolio Monday
content:
Fred Pedersen, the newest appointee to Nunavut’s cabinet, will receive his portfolio assignments on Monday, says Joanna Awa, press secretary for Premier John Main.




The Cambridge Bay MLA was selected by his colleagues on Nov. 5 to replace Brian Koonoo, who 

resigned

 from his ministerial duties on Nov. 2.




“I just want to thank the members again for putting their trust in me by selecting me to sit on the executive council,” Pedersen said in his Nov. 5 members statement to the legislative assembly.




“I want to assure my constituents in Cambridge Bay that I will continue to advocate on your behalf.”




He said as well that he’s looking forward to “in-depth” conversations with the premier, and finding out what portfolio he’d receive.




Koonoo was minister of environment, energy, languages and culture and heritage.




Cecile Nelvana Lyall, the minister responsible for the Nunavut Housing Corp., took on environment and energy in Koonoo’s absence. Human Resources Minister Annie Tattuinee took on the languages and culture and heritage assignments.
















Koonoo, the Tununiq MLA, listed a number of personal reasons for his resignation, including that he missed his family and hunting.

author: Corey Larocque
title: Nunavut recovery centre rooted in Liberal push to legalize cannabis
content:
Dennis Patterson




On Nov. 13, the Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre in Iqaluit will officially 

welcome

 the public in for the first time as part of an open house.




The striking facility overlooking the Apex River valley, for which local Stantec architect Joshua Armstrong was the team lead, is designed for healing in a traditional, trauma-informed way and has space to receive and prepare country food.










How did this building come to be? The drivers were the Senate of Canada, consultations in every Nunavut community and a last minute threat to delay the legalization of cannabis while eager investors salivated on Bay Street.




To understand the Senate’s pivotal involvement in this new facility, we have to go back to April 2017, when Bill C-45, to legalize cannabis, was introduced in Parliament, and the Senate Indigenous Peoples’ Committee was mandated to study the impact of the bill on Indigenous people.




As Nunavut’s representative in the Senate and a member of that committee, I visited every community in Nunavut to find out what people thought about the bill. We travelled in winter conditions in a single engine Pilatus PC-12.




My faithful and very capable work colleagues at the time were the late Leetia Nowdluk, who became interpreter/translator (although that was not in her job description as my executive assistant), and Claudine Santos, my director of parliamentary affairs. We went to schools, hamlet councils, and undertook consultations on community radio.
















The Cannabis C4-5 Consultation Tour in February and March of 2018 visited all 25 Nunavut communities (Graphic by Claudine Santos)




As I told the committee in testimony during consideration of the bill, I heard concerns everywhere from the public that for those who needed treatment for addictions, there was no facility in Nunavut.




Expert evidence in the committee showed that some people who are exposed to cannabis can develop serious disorders that require treatment: depression, anxiety and, in rare cases, schizophrenia.




Our committee report to the Senate highlighted the lack of access to culturally sensitive mental health and addictions services and that there was no treatment centre in Nunavut.




We quoted testimony from Arctic Bay elder Isaac Shooyook, who expressed fears about the lack of traditional knowledge-based prevention services in Nunavut. He recommended having “everything in place before you legalize it up there. There’s nothing in place to legalize cannabis in Nunavut.”




As a result of these and other concerns, our committee recommended to the Senate that the bill be amended to “delay the coming into force … for up to one year to allow time for: establishment of residential addictions treatment centres that are culturally and linguistically appropriate and in the vicinity of Indigenous communities” in the Yukon, N.W.T. and Nunavut.
















This recommendation landed in the Senate during what investment experts called “cannabis mania,” driven by the opportunity that Canada would become the first major G7 nation to legalize recreational cannabis.




Interest peaked through a mix of retail investor frenzy. New companies like Canopy Growth and Aurora Cannabis forecast quadrupling of their sales, and a Canadian company called Tilray Inc., which the Government of Nunavut later enlisted to sell mail-order cannabis through the Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission, saw its stock price soar, giving it a temporary higher value than Loblaws or Rogers.




Although the Trudeau government insisted that legalization of cannabis was not an economic initiative, it was about reducing social harm from black market drug dealers by improving regulation and quality control.




I believe that the government was also keenly aware of the excitement of investors in profiting from a new market.




At any rate, it was clear that a recommendation to delay Bill C-45 was not something the Trudeau government wanted to see happen. So on June 6, 2018, the bill came before the Senate for third and final reading.
















I had prepared and was poised to introduce an amendment to delay it. But the day before the final vote on Bill C-45 in the Senate, a letter came to the Indigenous Peoples’ Committee signed by two cabinet ministers committing $200 million for addiction treatment services and the promise of a report within 12 months of royal assent of the bill. As a result of that commitment, I withdrew my amendment and Bill C-45 passed.




Consultations on Bill C45 in Nunavut communities were undertaken in a single engine Pilatus PC 12 chartered aircraft, shown here in Pond Inlet during the tour. (Photo courtesy of Dennis Patterson)




On Oct. 3, 2018, former health minister Jane Philpott told the Indigenous Peoples’ Committee that she supported a wellness centre in Iqaluit.




Budget 2019 committed money for the design and building of the facility and annual operating funds. The GN offered to contribute 30 per cent towards capital costs and fund community based programming. Then-Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Aluki Kotierk committed money from Makigiaqta to fund Inuit counselling training. So the recovery centre became a three-way capital and operating funding partnership.




To make a difference in politics requires patience. Things don’t happen in a hurry. Nine years have passed since the Trudeau government announced the plan to legalize cannabis for recreational use.




It took pressure from Nunavut communities and some last-minute arm twisting in the Senate, a threat to delay the bill in order to trigger a federal commitment to build the much needed Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre.




The Hon. Dennis Patterson represented Nunavut in the Senate from 2008 to 2023. He was premier of the Northwest Territories from 1987 to 1991 and played a key role in the Nunavut land claim agreement.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Nunavik’s new sex-education curriculum takes shape
content:
Nunavik’s sexuality education pilot project will initially cover four subjects, including healthy relationships, pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections and contraception.




Kativik Ilisarniliriniq — Nunavik’s school board — and the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services 

rolled out the curriculum

 this month in Kuujjuaq and Umiujaq.




The program is intended for students from kindergarten to Grade 11 (Secondary V), with lessons adapted to their ages and stages of development.




At a Nov. 4 parent information session in Kuujjuaq, school commissioner Eva Kauki-Gordon said age appropriateness had been her main concern but after reviewing the material, she was satisfied that lessons would differ between grade levels.




Kauki-Gordon said she hopes the program will help young people feel more comfortable discussing their bodies and sexual health.




Growing up, she said, sexuality and puberty were rarely discussed at home. She recalled finding it difficult to speak to her mother about getting her first period.




“I think this would help for them to be more open,” she said of students.
















Five parents attended the Kuujjuaq information session. Kauki-Gordon encouraged more families to get involved in their children’s education.




“Be involved in the education that is being given,” she said. “You have [a] responsibility for your child.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut earns second-highest score from leading credit rating agency
content:
The Government of Nunavut received the second-highest possible credit score from Moody’s Ratings, a leading New York-based international credit rating agency.




The Aa1 rating was granted because the Canadian government financially backs the territory, according to the company’s report.




“This rating is an important milestone for Nunavut and reflects the strength of our financial position,” said Premier John Main, who is also finance minister, in a news release issued Monday. 

“It recognizes our government’s responsible financial management and the stability provided by our relationship with the Government of Canada.”




The company’s ratings system ranges from Aaa, the highest, to C, the lowest. 




Although Nunavut’s own-source revenue was only 17 per cent of total revenue in 2025-26, reflecting a narrow tax base due to its small population, the report concluded that there is “a high likelihood that the Government of Canada would provide extraordinary support should Nunavut face acute liquidity stress.”

title: Iqaluit Skating Club receives $5,000 grant
content:
The Iqaluit Skating club has $5,000 to spend after being named a recipient of this year’s Canada Post Community Grant.




Canada Post presented the grant to the local skating club on Monday morning at Astro Hill in Iqaluit.




Following the presentation of a $5,000 cheque, the Canada Post Community Foundation held an event for all attendees to celebrate the work that the Iqaluit Skating Club does for the community.




The non-profit distributes grants to schools, community organizations and other charities across the country that provide services for youth up to age 21.




The club provides programs and lessons and facilities for the community year round, with the grant aimed at supporting its inclusive skating programs.




The event also highlighted the importance and positive impacts created by community partnerships, according to Mahmooda Ahmed, who works for Canada Post.




This year, the Canada Post Community Foundation awarded over $1.3 million to 113 organizations across the country. The Iqaluit skating club was the only grant recipient from Nunavut.

title: Iqaluit observes Remembrance Day at cadet hall
content:
The cadet hall in Iqaluit was overflowing with about 300 people during the Royal Legion’s Remembrance Day ceremony Wednesday morning.




The annual event began around 11 a.m. in both English and Inuktitut.




“Canada as a nation owes an everlasting debt of gratitude to the men and women who have served and continue to serve their country, in times of war and peace,” said legion Branch 168 president John Graham,  the master of ceremonies.




The day began with a march that included police, veterans and community members. It began at the RCMP building on Sivumugiaq Street and ended at the hall.




RCMP chaplain Paul Hitz spoke about sharing gratitude for those who served.




“It is also a day to express our gratitude to those who serve today, the members of our Canadian Armed Forces, including our Canadian Rangers who stand guard over the ideals we as Canadians cherish,” he said. “Lest we forget.”




Hitz also acknowledged the youth who joined the ceremony and highlighted the significance of their presence.

author: David Venn
title: QIA considers ‘next steps’ after NIRB recommends hydro plant move forward without review
content:
The Qikiqtani Inuit Association is “considering its next steps” after the Nunavut Impact Review Board recommended that Iqaluit’s proposed hydro project move forward without a public review.




“Our priority remains ensuring that the development of new energy infrastructure advances alongside the protection of Inuit rights,” reads a statement from QIA spokesperson Markoosie Qaunirq, issued Tuesday.




The $500-million Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project, currently in its preliminary design phase, is proposed by Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp., a subsidiary of Qikiqtaaluk Corp., which is the QIA’s development arm.




If approved, it will lead to the construction of a hydroelectric plant able to produce up to 30 megawatts on the Kuugaaluk River, about 60 kilometres northeast of the city. It will also include a 7,136-hectare reservoir and a 66-kilometre access road.




NNC president Harry Flaherty has said the plant could replace 15 million litres of diesel fuel imported every year to generate electricity.




In November 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney named it a “nation-building” project to fast-track approvals. That move meant construction could begin in 2028 — two years earlier than originally anticipated.

title: Six hopefuls in running for Kitikmeot Inuit Association president
content:
Six candidates have put their name forward in the Kitikmeot Inuit Association’s presidential election.




The organization that manages lands in trust for Kitikmeot Inuit will elect its president, a vice-president and three regional board of directors on Dec. 14.




Two other Inuit organizations, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. and Qikiqtani Inuit Association, will also host their 

leadership elections

 the same day.




The KIA presidential nominees are Jeannie Ehaloak, Rosabelle Klengenberg and Lawrence Otokiak from Cambridge Bay; Simon Komangat and Raymond Quqshuun Sr. from Gjoa Haven; and David Audlatak Nivingalok from Kugluktuk, according to a news release from the organization.




Since late June, Nivingalok has served as acting president after KIA announced former president James Eetoolook had to take leave “for personal matters.”




James Aiyout, Abel Aqqaq, David Aqqaq, and Ashoona Iroqiut hope to be elected to the board to represent Taloyoak.




Kugluktuk and Kugaaruk have one person running for their community’s spot on the board of directors: Leah Kadlun put her name forward for the Kugluktuk seat, and Tars Angutingunirk put his name forward to represent Kugaaruk.
















The nomination period for KIA’s social and cultural vice-president position has been extended until Friday.




Successful candidates will hold onto their roles until 2030.

content:

title: Kuujjuaq festival organizer hopes to spark conversation about Inuit identity
content:
For organizer Saali Kuata, the Path to 100 Festival offers an opportunity to move beyond commemorating the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. It allows for Inuit to examine how it has shaped their communities.

The Path to 100 festival celebrates the 50th anniversary of the JBNQA and takes place at the Katittavik Theatre in Kuujjuaq from Sunday to Wednesday. It features an art exhibition, performances and workshops, as well as discussions about cultural identity, futurism and economic development.

author: David Venn
title: Preparations for Nunavut devolution entering ‘final phase,’ premier’s office says
content:
Preparations for devolution are entering “their final phase,” Nunavut Premier John Main’s office said Tuesday in a news release.




The release provides an update on the Government of Nunavut’s devolution process, which will see control over a vast majority of Crown land in the territory 

transferred

 to the GN.




To enable devolution, Nunavut must 

mirror

 six pieces of federal legislation: The Waters Act, Public Lands Act, Archaeological and Palaeontological Sites Act, Surface Rights Tribunal Act, Nunavut Planning and Project Assessment Act, and the Canada Oil and Gas Operations Act.




MLAs passed four of those acts through second reading during the fall sitting of the legislative assembly. They include the Waters Act, the Surface Rights Tribunal Act, Public Lands Act and Archaeological and Palaeontological Sites Act.




The final two bills will be tabled during the winter sitting, said the release.




Work is also ongoing to create a new Department of Mines, Natural Resources and Land. The department has a new organizational structure and Inuktitut name: Nunalirijikkut.




“Many Nunavummiut who will work in the new department are currently employed by the [federal government],” the release said, adding that the deadline for such employees to respond to the GN’s job offer is Nov. 22.
















“Their knowledge and technical expertise are highly valued.”

title: Expect office, road closures Wednesday for Remembrance Day
content:
Parts of downtown Iqaluit will be closed to traffic Wednesday morning to allow for a Remembrance Day ceremony and march to take place.




The closures will affect parts of Sivumugiaq Street and Mivvik Street starting at 9:30 a.m. until approximately 12 p.m., the City of Iqaluit announced Monday in a public service announcement.




“The closure is necessary to ensure the safety of participants and the public while the march is underway,” said the announcement.




The march, which starts at the RCMP detachment and ends at the cadet hall, is scheduled to start at 10:30 a.m.




Remembrance Day ceremonies are also planned in Rankin Inlet at the Singiituq Complex, from 10:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. and Cambridge Bay’s community hall at 10:30.




Government offices across the territory will also be closed to mark the day.




Remembrance Day is observed every year on Nov. 11 to honour armed forces members who have died in the line of duty.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit Northern store’s security guards get tactical makeover
content:
Iqaluit’s Northern store unveiled a 

new look

 in October, following three years of in-store renovations. Its security guards also got a makeover.




Some of their new all-black tactical uniforms come with accessories, including body-worn cameras and what appear to be retractable batons.




“Two guards per shift have cameras and they are only turned on during an event,” Brigitte Burgoyne, spokesperson for the North West Co., the Winnipeg-based parent corporation of Northern, said in an email.




“The North West Company does not collect body camera footage.”




Canadian Arctic Protective Services does, the company’s regional manager said.




That’s who North West Co. contracts for its security.




With a head office in Iqaluit, Canadian Arctic Protective Services provides security services across Nunavut, and in Ottawa and Yellowknife, “and soon in Miami, Florida,” its website says.
















“Footage access is limited to select management personnel and is used to review incidents and, where required, for law enforcement or legal proceedings,” said Paul Hunter, the security company’s regional director, in an email. 




“The cameras are turned on during an event and do not record continuously. They are not used for general customer surveillance.”




Hunter declined to say if the tool on the guard’s belt is a baton.




“We do not publicly share our internal security procedures or comment on site-specific security arrangements,” Hunter said.




Loblaws Inc., Canada’s largest food retailer, launched a pilot project using body cameras across B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario in early 2025. 

Shoppers Drug Mart followed.




“I take this as a completely misguided approach to the issue of food insecurity,” said sociologist Alissa Overend, interim director of the Research Institute of Urban Wellness at 

Edmonton’s MacEwan University, in a phone interview.
















“Even in cities, I don’t think policing is the right approach, but especially in northern and remote communities,” Overend said. “There have been criticisms of racial profiling.”




Shopper Marion Kusugak learned about some of the store’s on-site security arrangements first-hand on Thursday evening when a guard grabbed her backpack from her and then searched it, as she’d just begun shopping. 

(The guard who interacted with Kusugak is not the guard in the main photo of this story.)




Nunatsiaq watched as a 

guard dumped all her possessions on the checkout counter. 




“Be careful, please,” Kusugak said.




Some of her belongings fell to the floor as he rooted through them.
















Northern store shopper Marion Kusugak shows the red ticket a cashier gave her after her backpack was taken and searched by a security guard on Thursday evening. She was not wearing sunglasses and a hood when the guard stopped her. She wore them only for the photo. (Photo by Daron Letts)




When the search was over, the guard stuffed her things back in her backpack. Then the cashier took the bag and put it out of sight behind the counter and handed Kusugak a red ticket.




“It’s a new policy,” the cashier told her.




After a pause, Kusugak asked the guard his first name, then put her hand out to shake his. He didn’t shake her hand.




Asked how she felt about the search as she pushed her cart down the frozen food aisle, she said, “I didn’t like it.”




“This was a town first and then it became a city,” she said.




Burgoyne at North West Co., and Hunter at Canadian Arctic Protective Services declined requests to answer questions about whether the way the guard searched Kusugak’s backpack was standard practice or whether it was appropriate.




Down the street at Arctic Ventures, elder Seemeega Kootoo staffs the entrance six days a week. He is one of three local security guards at the store.




Iqaluit elder Seemeega Kootoo staffs the door at Arctic Ventures in Iqaluit on Wednesday evening. He is one of three local security guards at the store. (Photo by Daron Letts)




“When people who are barred from here come, I don’t let them in,” he said during an interview on Wednesday. “That’s what I do.”

When he is not busy, he returns shopping carts to their stall, he added.




Arctic Co-op stores use fixed in-store surveillance systems to address theft concerns “in the least invasive manner,” said company vice-president Duane Wilson. The company has also not adopted body-worn cameras for security staff because they require detailed policies around when to record, as well as accessing, storing and retaining footage.




Iqaluit RCMP have responded to an average of fewer than 10 shoplifting-related calls per month between January and October, said spokesperson Sgt. George Henrie.




On the North West Co. website, it states:




“In the spirit of Truth and Reconciliation, we acknowledge Canada’s colonial history and the policies of racism that created power imbalances throughout history and the resulting harm done to Indigenous Peoples,” under the heading: “Our promise to Indigenous Peoples.”

title: John Amagoalik seeks funding to stay in Nunavut while case winds through court
content:
Lawyers for John Amagoalik are scheduled to appear in court Friday in the hope of securing emergency funding that would allow him to stay in his home while his lawsuit against the Nunavut government proceeds.




Last month, the retired politician filed an

Amagoalik is revered by many as the “Father of Nunavut.” He dedicated decades of his life to advancing Inuit rights.




He had been living at the Embassy West long-term care home in Ottawa before returning to Iqaluit this summer. While his goal is to

The department has stated this type of funding

title: Rankin Inlet taxi service shuts down after nearly 6 years
content:
After nearly six years of driving residents around Rankin Inlet, Silu’s Taxi has closed.




Owner Silu Autut announced the closure Nov. 5 on Facebook, saying the cost of keeping vehicles on the road had become too much to justify continuing the service.




“The breakdowns and the cost of maintenance kept adding up, especially with what the cost of living is nowadays, and the long hours do catch up at the end,” Autut said to Nunatsiaq News in an interview conducted over Facebook Messenger.




Silu’s Taxi opened in February 2021, after the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.




“I started it for the town, to make sure the town is taken care of, not just to make money,” Autut said. 




The taxi operated daily, starting at 8 a.m. and usually running until at least 10 p.m. 




On Fridays and Saturdays, service often continued until midnight.
















“Sometimes, in the cold winter months or in the rain, we would pick up people walking by with an amauti carrying their infants, just to get them out of the cold and home safe,” Autut said.

ᒪᓕᒃᑐᒥ 2014−ᒥ ᐃᑭᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᒃᑯᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖓᓂ L’Isle-Verte−ᒥ ᑐᖂᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ 32−ᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ, ᑯᐸᐃᒃ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐱᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᕐᙲᓐᓇᑲᐅᑎᒋ ᐃᒥᕐᒥᒃ ᑎᖕᒥᑳᕈᑎᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᒃᑯᕕᖕᓂ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᕆᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᔪᓂ 10−ᓂ ᐅᓄᕐᓂᖅᓴᓂᒡᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ. ᐃᓱᓕᕝᕕᒃᓴᖓ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᓄᑦ ᒪᓕᒋᐊᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐅᖓᕙᕆᐊᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑎᓯᐱᕆ 2027−ᒧᑦ.

title: Police seize liquor, cash in Nunavik-Quebec investigation
content:
A man from Chambly, Que., and a woman from Kangiqsujuaq could face charges following a police investigation into the illegal possession and sale of alcohol.




The Sûreté du Québec’s Contraband Investigation Unit, working with the Nunavik Police Service, searched a property in Kangiqsujuaq on Wednesday. 




The investigation, which began in June, also led to a search in Chambly on Tuesday, after investigators determined the two cases were linked.




The searches resulted in the seizure of nearly eight litres of various alcoholic beverages and close to $12,000 in Canadian currency, according to a news release issued Thursday by the Quebec provincial police.




The individuals involved are a 34-year-old man from Chambly and a 32-year-old woman from Kangiqsujuaq. The news release did not provide their names. They could face charges related to illegal possession of alcohol and selling it without the required permits under Quebec’s Act respecting offences relating to alcoholic beverages.

title: Ottawa’s International Inuit Day brings communities together
content:
Clyde River seamstress Sarah Kiliktee had never seen a traditional sealskin tent before she helped build one in Ottawa.




Kiliktee travelled south to teach members of Ottawa-based Isaruit Inuit Arts how to construct an ittaq, a traditional Inuit tent made from sealskins.




Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk performs in Inuktitut for a crowd at Isaruit Inuit Arts’ sixth annual International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa on Saturday. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




The project began Oct. 26 and was completed 10 days later, just in time for Saturday’s International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa’s Sandy Hill neighbourhood, near the University of Ottawa.







Twenty-five sealskins were stitched together to make the tent that was on display at the park for visitors to step inside.




Kiliktee said the group of nine seamstresses relied on Google Images for reference because sealskin tents are no longer commonly used. They repeatedly checked measurements and patched holes around the flippers and tails of the skins.




“This is our first time and it turned out good, so we’re happy with it,” she said.
















Kiliktee said she came to Ottawa specifically for the celebration and was scheduled to leave early Sunday morning.

title: Six months to fix foster care failures is a tall order
content:
Six months isn’t much time to fix a problem that has festered for 15 years.




But that’s the task ahead for the Government of Nunavut after the federal auditor general presented a scathing report on the state of foster care in Nunavut, pointing to “fundamental weaknesses” that have persisted for years.




Deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes presented the report titled 

Foster Care in Nunavut

 on Tuesday. It’s the fifth time the office of the auditor general — responsible for probing the effectiveness of government programs — has looked into Nunavut’s foster care since 2011.




The Family Services Department can remove children from their family homes and place them in foster care when their parents aren’t able to meet their needs or provide a safe environment.

author: Randi Beers
title: Jimmy Bell – The ghost of Arctic Bay
content:
At Cape Dorset in 1949, Jimmy Bell, the large, fun-loving Hudson’s Bay Co. trader, took ill. His once rotund body began to waste away until he was but a shadow of his former self. 




On arriving in Cape Dorset, his young clerk, Peter Murdoch, who had known Jimmy in Lake Harbour, barely recognized him. He described him as “a skinny-looking fellow wearing baggy clothes, his face lined and his eyes a sickly yellow.”  




Officials in Winnipeg knew in February that Jimmy’s health was “not up to its usual robust standard,” but Jimmy attributed it to “too much of his own cooking.” 




In May he sent a message to Winnipeg that admitted he required medical attention. Another message followed, in which he said he would go out to Churchill on the supply ship for a check-up. But he kept the extent of his illness from his superiors. He surmised, correctly, that if they knew his true condition, they would evacuate him to the south. 




But Peter Murdoch knew that Jimmy needed attention, much more than he could provide using the post’s medical manual. He thought that Jimmy had stomach cancer. Without Jimmy’s knowledge, Murdoch sent a telegram by radio to Winnipeg informing them of Jimmy’s condition. Too late, Jimmy realized what Murdoch had done and mustered all his strength to roar at Murdoch and express his disapproval. 




Jimmy told Murdoch, “If I have cancer I want to die in the North. I want my spirit to stay in the North. When I die my spirit is going back to Arctic Bay. That’s the place I really love most – Arctic Bay.” 




But Winnipeg had got the message. Headquarters immediately dispatched their Canso aircraft, nicknamed Polar Bear, on the long flight to Cape Dorset.
















Jimmy was evacuated to Winnipeg on July 2. He was operated on at Winnipeg General Hospital a few days later, but doctors concluded that there was nothing more they could do for him. His mother and a brother were sent for and reached his bedside on the last day of August. Jimmy Bell died on Sept. 12 and was buried in Brookside Cemetery, in Winnipeg. He was only 43.




The inscription on his pink granite headstone ends with: “Here we leave our loved one sleeping.” 




But Jimmy wasn’t sleeping. He was restless. And, as he had promised, his spirit returned to Arctic Bay — or so it appeared.




Jimmy had a dear friend there. Amarualik was a leader among the Inuit and had worked for the Hudson’s Bay Co. for many years. Jimmy and Amarualik were close, and Jimmy had had a child with Amarualik’s daughter, Kautaq. That girl, Tapisa (now Tapisa Hughes of Arctic Bay) was the youngest of three daughters that Jimmy had with Inuit women.




When he died, the Hudson’s Bay Co. manager’s residence in Arctic Bay became the scene of strange occurrences. Residents and visitors heard footsteps in the storeroom, but there was no one there. Cups rattled in the cupboards and dishes rattled in the sink. But no one present had disturbed them. Doors mysteriously opened. The building was haunted.




Jimmy had returned to Arctic Bay to be near his old friend, Amarualik.
















It’s noteworthy that many of Jimmy’s manifestations happened in the kitchen of the residence, because Jimmy, in life, had apparently been obsessed with the neatness of his kitchen. Len Budgell, a lifelong Hudson’s Bay Co. employee, recalled that Jimmy was a bachelor and that “he liked things just so. If you did the dishes at night and hung the tea towel up, and it wasn’t the way Jimmy would have hung it up, in the morning you would find it neatly rearranged to Jimmy’s preference.” 




When the rattling of dishes became too loud, some company managers were known to shout, “Leave the bloody dishes alone, Jimmy.” 




That would generally result in a short burst of fierce rattling — Jimmy was clearly displeased — before silence would settle in. 




Soon after Eric Mitchell arrived in Arctic Bay as manager, he experienced a number of “curious, though disturbing incidents.” Footsteps were heard on the creaky floorboards of the attic night after night until one night he shouted, “Quit it!” 




One night he awoke to find all the doors of the house wide open. When he told Amarualik about these events, the old Inuk replied nonchalantly, “That’s just Jimmy Bell wandering around. Don’t worry about it; he’s just waiting for me to join him.” 
















The disturbances in Arctic Bay were no secret. They became part of Baffin Island lore. Word of the haunted staff house reached Winnipeg where some officials laughed it off. 




But one winter in the 1960s, company officials visited Arctic Bay and overnighted at the staff house. They wanted to investigate the reports of Jimmy’s ghost. Footsteps were said to have been heard on the roof, and so, on a windless night, they put a ladder up and spread flour on the roof, then waited. Sure enough, footsteps were heard again on the roof. But a physical check showed the flour undisturbed.




Amarualik passed away on June 28, 1967. The disturbances ceased at that time. Jimmy Bell’s friend had finally joined him, and Jimmy was finally at peace. 




Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: International Inuit Day celebration set to return to Ottawa’s Annie Pootoogook Park
content:
Isaruit Inuit Arts, an Ottawa-based organization, will host its sixth annual International Inuit Day celebration Saturday at Annie Pootoogook Park in the Sandy Hill neighbourhood. 




The event runs from noon to 4:30 p.m. and will feature musical performances, a feast, family games and cultural activities. It is free and open to the public. 




Performers include Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk, Ottawa-based drum dancer Donovan Gordon Tootoo, who is originally from Rankin Inlet, and the Nunavut Sivuniksavut students’ performing group.




Inuit arts and crafts vendors will also sell their work at the event.




The schedule includes a qulliq lighting at 1:30 p.m., performances from 1:40 p.m., a feast at 2:30 p.m. and community games at 3:15 p.m. 




An Inuit cultural activity tent will offer a qulliq making activity and photo opportunities featuring Inuit clothing.




International Inuit Day, observed annually on Nov. 7, was established by the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 2006 to celebrate Inuit culture and amplify Inuit voices across the circumpolar world.
















The date honours Greenlander Eben Hopson Sr., founder of the first Inuit Circumpolar Conference in 1977.

author: Daron Letts
title: MLAs wrap up fall sitting
content:
The fall sitting of Nunavut’s legislative Assembly wrapped up Thursday, with MLAs passing into law seven bills they introduced, leaving four to be dealt with later. 




“Thank you, each and every one of you, for working hard for the two weeks of what we did,” said Speaker David Joanasie, the MLA for South Baffin, as he closed the session at the end of the day.




MLAs looked at 11 bills over the two weeks that that they sat, beginning on Oct. 22, including legislation to increase the student loan limit, changes to the membership of the board of inquiry that governs medical professionals, and an approval for capital expenditures.




Among the bills that were passed were:







Bill 15: an act to amend the Student Financial Assistant Act to double the limit of loans made to a person who is eligible to receive other loans to $300,000.




Bill 14: an amendment to the Medical Profession Act to update the membership composition of the Board of Inquiry, set out term limits for members of the Board of Inquiry, establish hearing panels, and modernize the law’s language. 




Bill 10: Appropriation (Capital) Act, a bill that authorizes capital expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2028.







The policymakers are scheduled to return to the Legislative Assembly in the new year on Feb. 27.

title: Clyde River grieves hamlet councillor, victim of Iqaluit homicide
content:

Steven Aipellee, her brother, said she had been visiting Iqaluit with her partner when when she was fatally stabbed on Oct. 17.

title: Ottawa renews Inuit Child First Initiative funding, tops up Nutrition North
content:
The federal government is committing $575 million over five years to Inuit children’s services and more than $610 million over four years to northern food subsidies in this year’s federal budget.




The Liberal government released its budget for 2026-27, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” on Thursday.




It proposes renewing the Inuit Child First Initiative and transitioning it to Pirutsiagutiit, an Inuit-designed program developed with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami and the four Inuit treaty organizations.




The $575-million commitment would begin in the 2027-28 fiscal year. Pirutsiagutiit is expected to begin April 1, 2027, and will be operated by the treaty organizations or their designates, according to ITK.




Launched in September 2018, the Inuit Child First Initiative provides health, social, educational and other support to Inuit children and youth. Funding for the program ran out in 2025 and it 

has received

promise to retool

ITK had requested $600 million over five years for Pirutsiagutiit in its pre-budget submission.

author: Daron Letts
title: Experts decry Nunavut’s ‘Band-Aid’ approach to foster care
content:
The broken child welfare system in Nunavut is rooted in the territorial government’s colonial approach to the problem, say some with years of experience with the system.




“The taking of Indigenous children never stopped at residential school,” said Jeremy Young, who was separated from his mother as a child. “It only continued with foster care.”




Young spoke to Nunatsiaq News about his experience in Nunavut’s foster care system Thursday in response to the latest 

report

 by the federal auditor general

 i

nto the territorial government’s handling of youth in its care.




Tuesday’s report, the fifth over 15 years, shows little has changed. The Nunavut government is failing to account for the number of children in its care, failing to do consistent check-ins and failing in its duty to make sure every foster child is put into an appropriate home.




Young, now 26 years old, was taken from his mother as a child in Pangnirtung even though she did her best, Young said.




He blamed overcrowding and poverty for his family’s situation, saying his mother tried for 12 years to get housing for her family but ultimately could not.




“Society has failed Indigenous people,” he said. “That’s why we live in poverty. That’s why we go through the traumas we went through.”
















Young believes Inuit self-government is the antidote to the problems in the foster care system.

title: ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᕕᒃ ᓄᖅᑲᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᒥᐊᓗᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥᑦ. ᐱᒃᑲᖅᑎᑦᑎᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐱᖁᔭᐃᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᖅᑕᐅᓂᖏᓐᓄᑦ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see 

NuBrew stops canning, blames regulatory changes

.







ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᑏᑦ, ᐊᑕᐅᓯᑐᐊᖅ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᕕᒃ, ᓄᖅᑲᓚᐅᕐᒪᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᐅᑯᐊ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐃᒥᐊᓗᒃᒧᑦ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔩᑎᓪᓗᒋ ᖃᓄᖅ ᐃᒥᐊᓗᒃ ᐊᑭᓕᐅᑎᒃᓴᓕᐅᖅᑕᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂᒃ.




ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᕐᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᒪᑯᓄᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐃᒥᐊᓗᒃᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓱᐴᕐᑐᒐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᑎᒃᑯᓐᓄ 76 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᐊᑭᑭᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᕙᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᒪᑯᓇᙵᓪᓕ ᕕᐊᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒧᑦ ᑎᑭᑎᑕᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂᒃ. ᐱᒋᐊᖅᖢᓂ ᔫᓂ 1 ᑖᓐᓇ ᐊᔾᔨᒋᙱᔾᔪᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᒥᒃᖠᕚᓕᕈᑎᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ 40 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ.




“ᐊᔾᓕᒋᙱᔾᔪᑎᒋᔭᖓᓕ ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᕈᑎᒋᔭᕗᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᑯᐊ ᐊᖏᔪᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᕐᕕᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᐅᑯᑎᑐᓇᖅ ᐋᓐᕼᐊᐅᓱ-ᐳᔅ ᒥᒃᖠᕚᓪᓕᓚᐅᕐᒪᓐ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᔪᐊᑕᓐ ᑲᓇᑎ, ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᔭᐅᑲᐃᓐᓇᕐᑐᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᑎᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ.




“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐊᖏᔪᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᕐᕖᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᕙᙱᑦᑎᐊᕐᑐᑦ. ᐊᑭᓕᕐᓱᐃᕙᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᑭᓕᐅᑎᓂᒃ ᑖᒃᓰᔭᕈᑎᓂᒃ. ᐊᑭᓕᕐᓱᐃᕙᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒋᔭᐅᔪᒥᒃ. ᐃᓄᖕᓂᓪᓗ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᑦᑎᕙᙱᖢᑎᒃ. ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᑎᒍᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖃᑦᑕᙱᑦᑐᑦ ᐅᕙᑦᑎᑐᑦ.”




ᑲᓇᑎ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓕᓚᐅᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᑭᒋᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᓄᕐᓯᕚ9ᓕᕐᓂᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᓇᒻᒪᒃᓴᙱᑦᑐᖃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᒫᓂ $120-ᓂ ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᖃᑦᑕᐅᔭᕆᔭᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᓂᐅᕕᕐᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᕘᓇ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᕕᐊᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᕗᐊᐃᓂᒥ ᓂᐅᕕᕐᕕᖕᓂ ᔪᓚᐃ ᐃᓱᓕᓕᕐᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᑲᓇᑎ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐅᖃᖃᑎᖃᓕᕋᒥ ᐊᐅᔭᖅ ᐃᓱᓕᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᑭᐅᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐅᕆᔭᐅᓇᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᕐᒥᒃ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᑕᖏᑦᑕ ᓴᙱᓂᖏᑦ ᒥᒃᖠᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᓗᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ.
















ᐅᓇ ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᓗᐊᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᕐᓯᒍᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᓚᖓ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐃᒥᐊᓗᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓱᐴᕐᑐᒐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᑭᓕᐅᑎᐅᖃᑦᑕᕋᔭᖅᑐᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᕕᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᒪᓐ ᐊᑭᓕᐅᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᒪᓕᒋᐊᖃᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐃᒥᐊᓘᑉ ᓴᙱᓂᖓᓄᑦ.




ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂᓪᓕ ᐅᓇ ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᖅ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᒪᓐ ᐃᒪᖅᑯᖅᑐᓂᖓᒍᑦ. ᒫᓐᓇᓕ 355 ᒥᓕᓖᑕ ᐃᐳᐃᑦᑐᖅ ᕕᐊ 3..5 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᓴᙱᓂᖃᕐᓗᓂ ᓲᕐᓗ ᒪᑯᑎᑐᓇᖅ ᑯᕉᓇ ᓚᐃᑦᑎᑐᑦ, ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᕈᑎᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᖕᒪᑕ $1.46. 6 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᓴᙱᓂᓕᒃ ᐊᑭᓂᖓ ᐊᔾᔨᒋᓪᓗᓂᐊ ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᖅᑕᐅᔾᔪᑎᖃᕐᒪᑕ $2.50-ᒥ

title: Nunavut’s addictions treatment centre to open its doors for tour next week
content:
Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre will open its doors to the public for the first time next week in an open house.




Health Minister Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster announced the event in a minister’s statement in the legislative assembly Wednesday.




She announced the open house, hosted by the territorial government, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., and Indigenous Services Canada, will take place on Nov. 13, but did not announce a time.




“This will be an opportunity for Nunavummiut to tour Aqqusariaq and recognize the people and partnerships behind it,” Brewster said.




The $87-million Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre is located across from the Arctic Winter Games Arena in Iqaluit.




Planning for the facility has been 

underway

 for more than a decade, Brewster said during her statement, and while “substantial completion” of the building is done, more work is needed before the facility can begin taking in patients.




The official opening date has yet to be announced, and the Inuit-led not-for-profit 

tasked with operating

 the facility will announce it when Aqqusariaq is ready for intake to begin, said Brewster.

title: Search called off for missing Gjoa Haven elder
content:

The Hamlet of Gjoa Haven has called off a search for an elder who went missing two weeks ago.




On the morning of Oct. 21, 84-year-old David Siksik left home on his Honda ATV without a satellite messenger device to set fishing nets at a lake about 32 kilometres north of the community.




He never returned home, though his son,

 Allen Siksik, still believes he might.




“I do have hope,” Siksik said in an interview Thursday. “I still have hope, thinking he is waiting in a cabin, but no one could find even the ATV.”




Over 13 days, searchers travelled by ATV within 100 kilometres of Gjoa Haven, the hamlet said in a Nov. 3 update on Facebook.




A Canadian Coast Guard helicopter and a Royal Canadian Air Force Hercules aircraft assisted. Community members organized ground searches, including trips to Peel Inlet, on the northern coast of King William Island.
















The neighbouring community of 

Taloyoak pitched in fuel, Siksik said.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Quebec coroner looking into death of Inuk girl
content:
A Quebec coroner is investigating the death of a four-year-old Inuk girl who died while under the supervision of Montreal’s youth protection services.




The girl, whose mother is from Nunavik, died in a hospital on March 31, after a worker at Batshaw Youth and Family Centres failed to respond to a request for an urgent visit at her family home, according to reporting by 

Radio-Canada.




“We can confirm that an investigation into the causes and circumstances of this death is being conducted,” said Jake Lamotta Granato, a spokesperson for Quebec’s coroner’s office, in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




Coroner Steeve Poisson has been assigned to the case, Lamotta Granato said.




“At the end of his investigation, should he deem it appropriate, the coroner may also issue recommendations aimed at protecting human life and preventing deaths under similar circumstances,” he said.




In late July, Santé Québec, which oversees health and social services in the province, announced it had ordered its inspection office to investigate the quality of youth protection services offered under its agency for Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal — Universitaire area, which has jurisdiction over Batshaw.




The announcement about the investigation came days after the Montreal Gazette revealed three youth under Batshaw’s care — including the four year old girl — had 

died suddenly in March

.

title: GN plans new bidding process to run Ottawa medical boarding home
content:
The Government of Nunavut plans to issue a new request for proposals for the operation of Larga Baffin, a boarding home for Inuit travelling to Ottawa for medical reasons.




The move is the latest in protracted negotiations between Larga Baffin Ltd., the facility’s current operator, and the territorial government, and could affect 

expansion plans

 for the facility.




Larga Baffin submitted a response to the GN’s initial request for proposals, which closed in May 2024, to operate the boarding home, but no contract was awarded, company president Malaya Zehr said in an Oct. 29 email to Nunatsiaq News.




The proposed contract was to run for 20 years, with two optional five-year renewal periods, for a potential total of 30 years.




The long-term agreement was intended to help a succe1ssful bidder secure financing to obtain or build a facility that met the capacity requirements, said former Nunavut health minister John Main two years ago in the legislative assembly.




For years Larga Baffin has been 

working through

 Ottawa’s municipal planning process to build a 

six-storey, 220-room facility at Hunt Club Road and Sieveright Avenue — about five kilometres northeast of the the Ottawa airport — that would accommodate up to 350 guests.




The existing facility on Richmond Road can hold 195 guests.
















Larga Baffin bought the Hunt Club Road property in 2020.

title: Tuberculosis documentary shows healing through sharing stories
content:
Iqaluit’s Astro Theatre was filled with people Tuesday evening for the première of a documentary that follows a group of tuberculosis survivors and youth as they find closure over their forced relocations decades ago.




Between the 1940s-1960s, the federal government transported thousands of Inuit to southern sanatoriums for tuberculosis treatment without their consent or without informing them about what was happening.




Many Inuit never returned home.




Taqqut Productions joined hands with The SeeChange Initiative to create 

Our Elders are so Important to Us: A Tuberculosis Sanatorium Healing Journey

, a 29-minute documentary that follows youth and survivors as they connect over these relocations, in an effort to provide healing and closure.




“If we value our elders as much as we say we do as Inuit, why not listen to their stories,” asked Naomi Tatty, the intercultural health lead at SeeChange, a non-profit and one of the leads for the documentary.




“Why not put their words out there and help us younger generations, and the generations ahead of us, understand what our families went through?”




She was on site for the screening and to help facilitate discussion afterwards, at the Storehouse.

title: Nunavut to receive $65.3M in additional federal funding for housing
content:
Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. will receive $65.3 million in federal funding for Inuit housing over five years, an expenditure MP Lori Idlout says is welcome but must be part of a long-term commitment to address the territory’s housing crisis.




“I know that when I still go to the communities, housing is always the first thing that’s mentioned to me as an important issue,” Idlout said in an interview Wednesday. 

“It’s great to see our government hearing that.”




The funding comes from a $130.3-million top up to the federal government’s Urban, Rural and Northern Indigenous Housing Strategy, which Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty announced Oct. 30 in Kuujjuaq.




The money will go to the four Inuit Treaty Organizations, including $32.5 million to Makivvik, nearly $17 million to the Inuvialuit Regional Corp. and $15.5 million to the Nunatsiavut Government.




The federal government previously allocated $197.5 million, bringing the total to $327.8 million, according to the government’s news release.

title: Ikur’raq cabin program expands with $500,000 in federal money
content:
The federal government has topped up a cabin program meant to reduce homelessness in Nunavut, Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok announced Oct. 27.




Close to $514,000 will go towards the territory’s Ikur’raq Cabins Initiative, a project meant to give people a temporary place of respite from overcrowding, violence and addiction issues. The money will fund 15 cabins.




“Out-of-shelter homelessness is a major public health and safety issue,” Akearok said in her minister’s statement at the legislative assembly. “The Ikur’raq cabins offer a practical response to this urgent need.”




The GN funded the 

first set of 16 cabins

 in 2022 and the program was revived in 2025 with $1 million in federal money to build 20 additional cabins.




Akearok’s Oct. 27 announcement will bring the total to 51.




Hamlets, non-profits and hunters and trappers organizations can apply for $50,000 grants with the new round of funding.




The original 16 cabins include three Pangnirtung, two each in Arviat and Pond Inlet, and one cabin in each of Coral Harbour, Iqaluit, Clyde River, Naujaat, Baker Lake, Igloolik, Kugaaruk, Taloyoak, and Kugluktuk.
